title: Cookie
explain: A cookie is one name=value string that the server asks the browser to keep with Set-Cookie, and that the browser then attaches automatically to every matching request. It is the only browser storage the server sees on every request, which is why it carries session IDs and why it is a poor place for bulk data.
model:
A cookie is **one** `name=value` string. A request can carry several: `Cookie: session_id=abc123; theme=dark`.

**Identity is the triple (name, Domain, Path).** Two cookies coexist if they share a domain but differ in name or path:

```http
Set-Cookie: session=abc; Domain=example.com; Path=/
Set-Cookie: session=xyz; Domain=example.com; Path=/admin
```

A request to `/admin/users` sends both; `/home` sends only the first.

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `Domain`, `Path` | scope; with no `Domain` the cookie is host-only |
| `Expires` / `Max-Age` | persistent; without them a **session cookie**, dropped when the browser session ends |
| `Secure` | HTTPS only |
| `HttpOnly` | invisible to JavaScript, blunts XSS theft |
| `SameSite=Lax/Strict/None` | limits cross-site sending, the main CSRF defence |

Limits: about 4 KB each, and every byte rides on every in-scope request. Use cookies for small identifiers (an opaque session ID, a signed token); keep the rest on the server or in [localStorage](#/sd/f/local-storage).

details.q: The browser holds `session=abc; Path=/` and `session=xyz; Path=/admin` for example.com and requests `/admin/users`. What does the Cookie header contain?
details.a: Both, since both path scopes match; by convention the more specific path comes first, but the server should not depend on the order. A request to `/home` carries only `session=abc`. Name, domain and path make them distinct cookies.

details.q: Which attributes do you set on a banking session cookie?
details.a: `Secure` (never over plain HTTP), `HttpOnly` (injected scripts cannot read it), and `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` (limits cross-site requests carrying it). Leave `Domain` unset so it stays host-only; setting `Domain=example.com` shares it with every subdomain, including a neglected one.

details.q: Why not put a lot of data in cookies?
details.a: Every byte is uploaded on every matching request, including images and scripts. A page that makes 60 requests with 3 KB of cookies uploads 180 KB, none of it useful for static assets. Serve static files from a cookieless domain or keep cookies tiny.

details.q: Where should the session ID live for a server-rendered app that must know the user on the first navigation?
details.a: In a cookie: only cookies travel with navigations by themselves, before any script has run. localStorage is invisible to the server until JavaScript copies it; query parameters leak into logs and referrers.

Cookies are sent to the server on every matching request, readable by the server (and by scripts unless `HttpOnly`), about 4 KB each. localStorage is never sent, readable only by same-origin scripts, about 5 MB. Cookie for small server-visible identifiers; localStorage for client-only preferences and caches.

details.q: What is the trade-off between a cookie and a token in localStorage for authentication?
details.a: A token in localStorage can be read by any script on the page (XSS). An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot, but because the browser attaches it automatically you must defend against CSRF with `SameSite` and tokens. Pick the risk you can control better.

A session cookie has no `Expires`/`Max-Age` and is dropped when the browser session ends (browsers that restore sessions may keep it). A persistent cookie lives until its expiry; use it for remember-me with a revocable token on the server side.

prompts.q: Explain what a cookie is and what makes it different from other browser storage.
points: One name=value string set via Set-Cookie
The only storage the server sees on every request
Small: about 4 KB, each byte on every request

prompts.q: How is a cookie identified, and what happens with two cookies of the same name?
points: Identity is name, Domain and Path
Different path means two cookies coexist
Both sent when both scopes match

prompts.q: Secure a session cookie and say what each attribute defends against.
points: Opaque ID or signed token, short lifetime
